defaults.teacher_persona: A prompt engineer who writes briefs for a living and judges every prompt by whether a colleague could reproduce the result.
classmates: An operations coordinator who writes prompts by trial and error
A compliance-minded editor who asks what the prompt lets the model get away with
defaults.interaction: Live lab: the teacher rewrites one weak prompt in public, then the peers rewrite their own and test each other's.
defaults.assessment: Each classroom ends with 3-5 checks aligned to the chapter's graded activity.

classrooms.title: A Brief, Not a Wish
classrooms.prompt: Put four vague workplace prompts on the board ('write an email about the delay', 'summarize this', 'make a plan', 'improve this'). The teacher rewrites the first one live into a brief with context, audience, constraints, an example of good output, and a definition of done, then explains each added line. The classmates rewrite the remaining three and test them against a supplied source document, comparing outputs. Include slides on the five parts of a usable brief, a roleplay where the model returns something technically correct but useless, and a quiz on which prompt is more likely to be reproducible. Close with a template learners can paste into their own tools.
objectives: Write a brief with context, constraints, and a definition of done
Give an example of good output instead of adjectives
Judge whether a prompt is reproducible by a colleague

activities.title: The five parts of a brief

classrooms.title: Critique, Revise, Constrain
classrooms.prompt: Run an iteration lab: the class starts from a mediocre AI draft of a one-page procedure. The teacher demonstrates a critique loop (list what is wrong, ask for a revision that fixes only those points, then constrain the format), and the peers run three rounds on their own draft, keeping a short log of what each change fixed and what it broke. Include a segment on when to stop iterating because the model is drifting, a roleplay where a colleague keeps asking for 'better' without saying what better means, and a quiz on the next move for four stalled prompts. End with the iteration log template.
objectives: Critique a draft against explicit criteria
Revise one attribute at a time and keep a log

classrooms.title: AI in the Tools You Already Use
classrooms.prompt: Work through a day of office tasks in the productivity suite: drafting an email thread, turning meeting notes into decisions and owners, building a spreadsheet formula, and summarizing a long document. For each, the teacher shows the task, the prompt, the review gate, and the failure mode, then the peers do one task with a supplied source and compare results. Include a roleplay where an AI-written email contains a promise the organization cannot keep, and a quiz on which outputs need a second reader. Emphasize that the tool's convenience never removes the review gate.
objectives: Use AI inside email, documents, and spreadsheets with a review gate
Turn notes into decisions and owners

activities.title: Who reads this before it sends

classrooms.title: A Prompt Library Your Team Can Trust
classrooms.prompt: Have the class turn individual prompts into a shared library: a name, the job it does, the prompt text, an example input, an example good output, the review gate, and the owner who keeps it current. The teacher shows a prompt that silently broke when a tool changed and explains versioning and test cases. The peers review two library entries for missing context or an unsafe default, then rewrite one. Include slides on library hygiene, a roleplay where a colleague copies a prompt from the internet into a restricted workflow, and a short assessment on what a trustworthy entry must contain.
objectives: Turn a working prompt into a documented library entry
Add a test case and an owner to each entry
Refuse an untrusted prompt in a restricted workflow
